conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your surgical team members. You're here today for placement of a peritoneal dialysis catheter, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been on hemodialysis, but I’d like to try peritoneal dialysis if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we’re doing this. We’ll place the catheter laparoscopically today and also take care of some adhesions we expect to find.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a lot of surgeries before. Is this going to be risky?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your complex history, including lupus and past transplants. The surgery itself went well. You were in the OR for about an hour and a half, mostly due to extensive adhesions, but the catheter is in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well post-op. We’ve started you on antibiotics just in case, and we’ll monitor your incision and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little warm. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your temperature is slightly elevated at 101.2. It’s common after surgery. We’ll keep an eye on it and make sure it doesn’t go higher.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your fever is still present—101.6 this morning. We’ve started you on Levaquin as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t see signs of infection yet. Blood cultures and peritoneal fluid tests came back negative. The fever may just be a post-op reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We accessed it and saw some bloody fluid, which is expected after surgery. We’re flushing it gently to keep it clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You completed your hemodialysis session this afternoon. You tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about how I’d feel after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fever is still around 101.4. We did a chest X-ray because of the fever—shows some atelectasis, which means parts of your lungs aren’t fully inflated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not usually. We’ll encourage deep breathing and nebulizers to help open up your lungs. It often improves with time and activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing the breathing exercises. Should I walk more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, walking helps a lot. We’d like you to get up and walk a few times a day to prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your hematocrit is dropping slowly—from 31.6 to 29.8. We’re going to give you a unit of blood to stabilize it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. The bloody fluid from the catheter suggests some internal oozing. It’s not severe, but we want to keep your levels stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your levels tomorrow. One unit should be enough if things stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your hematocrit stabilized after the transfusion. It’s now 30.1. The catheter flushes are clearer too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. My fever is gone, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your last temperature was 99.8. You’re defervescing, which is excellent. We’ll continue the antibiotics for a full 7-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last night, the monitor went off. They said something about a heart rhythm issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, telemetry showed what looked like ventricular fibrillation, but your vitals were stable, and you had no symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Was it a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology reviewed it and believes it was an artifact—likely a monitor glitch. Your EKG was normal, and cardiac enzymes were fine. No treatment changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I was really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also restarting your Coumadin. It was held because your INR was high at 4.1. Now we’re starting you on a lower dose—1 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need that for my anticardiolipin syndrome, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It helps prevent clots. We’ll monitor your INR closely, especially while you’re on antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Abdominal pain is improving, you’re eating, and walking more. We’ll plan for discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I start peritoneal dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You’ll continue hemodialysis for now. The PD nurse will see you next week for training and initial flushes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You’ll need to keep the site dry until the PD nurse gives you specific instructions, likely next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All labs look stable. Hematocrit is holding at 27.5, white count is down, and kidney function is as expected for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tomorrow. We’ll go over discharge instructions, medications, and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged home. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and everything is healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the clinic if you have fever over 101, chills, increased abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or trouble keeping food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the catheter site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it clean and dry. No showering yet. The PD nurse will guide you on care next week. No heavy lifting for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Keep your appointments, take your meds, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my constipation has been worse since surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added docusate, senna, and lactulose. Drink plenty of fluids and try to stay active. Use the suppository if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge meds are ready. Warfarin 1 mg daily, Levaquin every 48 hours for three doses, and all your usual meds are included.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take them as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will review your instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—I continue hemodialysis on my regular schedule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Per your usual routine. The PD transition will be gradual and guided by the nurse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds—are they adjusted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lisinopril is now 20 mg daily, and amlodipine is 10 mg total—two 5 mg tablets. We adjusted based on your pressures in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep following up and taking care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in with high blood pressure and vision changes—can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I took my blood pressure at home and it was 201 over 112. I took one 50mg hydralazine, but it didn’t help much. My doctor told me to take another, but it was still high, so I came to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned seeing flashing colored lights—did that last long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a few hours. But it went away after I got to the ER. No blurry vision or loss of sight, just the lights.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. That can happen with very high blood pressure. We did a head CT, and there’s no bleeding or stroke—so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank you. That was scary. I’ve had it before when my BP spikes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history of malignant hypertension and posterior leukoencephalopathy makes you more prone to this. We’ll work on getting your BP under better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking all my meds. I only take lisinopril on non-dialysis days because I get low BP after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s smart. But your BP has stayed in the 150s to 170s systolic since admission. We’re going to increase your lisinopril to 40mg daily and add hydralazine 25mg four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is that safe with my other medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve reviewed everything. We’re keeping your amlodipine, metoprolol, and other BP meds the same. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also had low-grade fevers at night for the past two days. Temperature hit 100.4.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. We’ve drawn blood, urine, and peritoneal fluid cultures to check for infection. Your chest X-ray is clear, no signs of pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had loose stool this morning, but no nausea or vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. Your labs don’t show signs of severe infection. White count is normal, and lactate is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had some belly pain this morning—dull, all over. But it went away after a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdomen is soft, no guarding. We checked your peritoneal fluid—WBC is slightly elevated at 138, but no organisms on gram stain. Culture is pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing PD training—getting used to the fluid exchanges.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. The fluid you drained yesterday had a little blood, but that’s not uncommon early on. We don’t think this is peritonitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also have genital herpes—started three days ago. I’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that on exam. It’s likely a reactivation. We’re starting acyclovir 400mg daily for five days. That should help it resolve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but herpes usually doesn’t cause fever this long. We’ll keep monitoring. If fevers persist, you should call your PCP after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your cultures are back—blood, urine, and peritoneal fluid all show no growth. So no active infection we can find.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the fevers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to your lupus or just a mild viral process. Since everything’s negative, we don’t think you need antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still on prednisone from my transplant—should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing it for now. But you should discuss with your renal doctor why you’re still on it since the transplant failed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Coumadin? My INR was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 1.5 on admission—below goal. We’re increasing your dose to 3mg daily. You’ll get your INR checked at your next dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I don’t want another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. With your antiphospholipid syndrome, staying anticoagulated is very important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. You’re afebrile now, BP is stable in the 150s/80s, and labs are improving. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lisinopril is now 40mg daily, hydralazine 25mg four times a day, Coumadin is 3mg daily, and you’ll finish the acyclovir for herpes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I should check my BP at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice daily. Call your doctor if it’s over 160/100, or if you have headache, chest pain, or vision changes again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the fevers come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your PCP if fever goes above 100.4, or if you develop chills, shortness of breath, or stomach pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ll follow up with your renal doctor soon. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I came in because my INR was really high—like 19. I fell a few days ago and broke my ankle, but they didn’t check my blood then. I’ve been feeling off since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your INR was dangerously high. That means your blood is too thin. Did you change your warfarin dose recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been taking 3 mg daily like always. The only new thing is Percocet for my ankle pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you vitamin K and fluids to reverse the effect. We’re also watching for any signs of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did vomit dark red blood that morning. And I’ve had blood when I blow my nose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We saw you were guaiac positive, meaning there’s blood in your stool. But your hemoglobin is stable, so no active major bleed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the warfarin? Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We paused it for now. Hematology thinks you don’t need a heparin bridge since your transplant failed. We’ll restart carefully later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been confused. I forgot I needed dialysis one day. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about that. Your labs show high potassium and kidney failure, which can affect brain function. Nephrology is adjusting your dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing peritoneal dialysis at home. It’s been harder since the fall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a dialysis treatment today. Your potassium was 6.9, which is dangerous. We gave insulin and sugar to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I felt weak and lightheaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s from the high potassium and low blood pressure. We’re giving fluids and watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR is down to 1.2 now—much safer. But we’re still not sure why it spiked so high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be the new warfarin pills? I got a refill last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We suggest not using that bottle and getting a new prescription. Pill count showed you actually underdosed, so it’s confusing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I use a weekly pillbox. Maybe I mixed up old and new bottles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could happen. We’ll restart warfarin at a lower dose and monitor closely. Your GI team also recommends staying on high-dose pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heartburn since I started dialysis. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s common. We’ve increased your pantoprazole to twice daily to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last night I had sharp chest pain and shoulder blade pain. I got really anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a chest X-ray and ECG. No heart or lung issues. It was likely from your full dialysis bag pressing on your diaphragm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I felt better after draining it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Anxiety can make it feel worse. We’ll keep your dialysis schedule consistent to avoid that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your chest CT. No signs of bleeding or infection. Your lungs look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried because of my past lung bleeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. But this scan is reassuring. Your main issues are the high INR, GI bleed, and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel a little shaky in my hands. Is that from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Ziprasidone can cause tremors. Since you’re on long-term steroids, it was started for mood stability. We’ll consider adjusting it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. I’m not manic, just anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss with your psychiatrist. For now, we’re keeping your other depression meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your INR is stable, potassium is normal, and you’re not bleeding. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take six 1 mg tablets for the next two nights—so double dose—to catch up. Then go back to three. Follow up with your clinic in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds? I was on metoprolol and lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take half your metoprolol this weekend. Resume full dose after talking to your doctor. Lisinopril is back on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I get an endoscopy for the stomach bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not urgent now. Discuss it with your GI doctor as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my constipation? I’ve been using lactulose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding senna and docusate to help. Keep using lactulose as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Just keep up with dialysis, take your meds as directed, and follow up closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon. You can go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me about the chest pain that brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started last night. It’s a squeezing pain in my chest that goes up to my neck and shoulders. It got worse when I breathed in or moved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you have any shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt nauseous, but no sweating or trouble breathing. I took Percocet and Gaviscon, but nothing helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You said you got some relief with nitroglycerin in the ambulance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a little. But I also took two Percocets, so I’m not sure what helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ve done some tests. Your EKG showed sinus tachycardia and some ST elevations, but your cardiac enzymes were normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the enzymes are negative, which is reassuring. But we did find something else. An echocardiogram showed a small amount of fluid around your heart — a pericardial effusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fluid around my heart? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and there’s no sign of pressure on the heart, so it’s not an emergency. But we need to figure out why it’s there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be from my lupus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. Lupus can cause pericarditis — inflammation of the lining around the heart. We’ve consulted rheumatology to help us decide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had fevers too. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fever and the elevated white blood cell count suggest inflammation. We’re checking your dialysis fluid and blood cultures to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My dialysis has been tricky lately. The fluid isn’t staying in very long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with nephrology. They recommend shorter 3-hour dwells instead of 4, since longer ones lead to reabsorption. We’ll increase the number of dwells to improve clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been feeling more swollen too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan showed new ascites — fluid in your belly — which might be related to your dialysis or inflammation. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the chest pain from the fluid or the lupus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know for sure. It could be lupus-related pericarditis or a viral cause. But since your lupus markers aren’t strongly suggestive of a flare, we’re leaning toward treating it as inflammatory.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean for treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to increase your prednisone from 5mg to 30mg daily to reduce the inflammation. If it’s pericarditis, this should help your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on steroids before. Will I have side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly — increased appetite, trouble sleeping, or mood changes. But we’ll taper it over four weeks back to your usual 5mg, which should minimize that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. What about my warfarin? My last INR was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Your INR has been rising, and with inflammation around the heart, there’s a risk of bleeding into the pericardium. We’ve held your warfarin and given vitamin K.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not on blood thinners now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll restart it at a lower dose once your INR is stable and the inflammation improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood and dialysis fluid cultures came back negative. No infection found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The fever and high white count were probably due to inflammation from the pericarditis. Your temperature is normal now, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My chest pain is better. Still there, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The prednisone is likely helping. We’ll keep monitoring your symptoms and repeat the echo if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your BUN is coming down. That means your dialysis is working better with the shorter dwells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less bloated too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep this schedule and have you follow up with your nephrologist to optimize your clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my mood? I’ve been feeling down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on citalopram, mirtazapine, and ziprasidone. We’ll keep those the same unless you’re having side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’re helping. Just more tired than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mirtazapine can cause drowsiness. We can adjust the dose if needed, but for now, it’s okay to keep it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The latest chest X-ray shows no change in the effusion. Your pain is much better, and you’re afebrile. I think we’re moving in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, possibly tomorrow. We’ll discharge you on 3mg of warfarin, continue the prednisone taper, and keep your other meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to see my rheumatologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to review the pericarditis and adjust your lupus management. Also, your nephrologist will help fine-tune your dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, no fever, pain is minimal. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have worsening chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, or swelling. Keep taking your meds, especially the prednisone taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Restart at 3mg daily. Your INR will need close monitoring — follow up with your anticoagulation clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make the appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on omeprazole twice a day to protect your stomach, especially with the steroids. And keep using senna and docusate for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using lactulose at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. Just make sure you’re not overusing it. Stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — the air under my diaphragm on the X-ray. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s likely from your dialysis. Small amounts of air can get in during the exchange. It’s not dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But everything looks good. You’re safe to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what happened that brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I passed out twice last night when I went to the bathroom. I woke up on the floor both times. The second time, I hit my nose and it bled a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Were you feeling lightheaded before you passed out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very lightheaded and weak. I also felt nauseous but didn’t throw up. I wasn’t straining or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I understand your dialysis fluid was increased recently, and you started Miralax. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my PD nurse said my ultrafiltrate was low and wanted to ‘clean me out.’ But I wasn’t constipated. Now I’ve had loose stools all night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be why you fainted. The fluid shift and diarrhea may have caused dehydration and low blood pressure when you stood up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it wasn’t my heart or something serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your heart with an EKG and blood tests. No signs of heart attack. Your enzymes were slightly elevated, but that’s common in kidney disease. Telemetry showed no dangerous rhythms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my nose? It still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan shows a small fracture in your left nasal bone. But you’re breathing fine and oxygen levels are good. ENT recommends follow-up as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. My hip also hurts from falling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We examined your hip. No signs of fracture. It’s likely bruised. You’re walking okay now, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been feeling more tired than usual the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve gained some weight from fluid overload. That’s why your dialysis was increased. But it may have caused too much fluid removal overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the Miralax and dialysis together made me pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The combination likely led to dehydration and low blood pressure when you stood up—what we call orthostatic hypotension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I didn’t realize that could happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve adjusted your dialysis prescription per your nephrologist’s recommendations to avoid this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my lupus and other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on prednisone 15mg daily. No need for stress doses. We continued your other lupus and kidney meds like lisinopril and sevelamer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood thinner? I’m on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was up to 2.6. We’re changing your warfarin to 3mg every day instead of alternating doses. You’ll follow up to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram to check the fluid around your heart. You had a pericardial effusion before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, from my last admission. Was it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there but looks more consolidated, especially in front of the right ventricle. No signs of tamponade. But we want to watch it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that cause problems?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If it thickens, it could restrict heart function. Your nephrologist and PCP know, and you’ll need a follow-up echo in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to go. Is the fluid infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your dialysis fluid. No white blood cells or bacteria. So no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. My chest hasn’t hurt, so I’m glad it’s not that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no chest pain or shortness of breath is reassuring. Your lungs look clear on X-ray except for mild atelectasis, which is common after lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It’s been high lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your blood pressure meds temporarily but restarted amlodipine and lisinopril. Your BP is stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home tomorrow if all stays well. We’re changing your prednisone to 15mg daily—three 5mg tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, I was on 15mg before. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’re keeping it the same. And omeprazole twice a day for your reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any last instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Take warfarin 3mg daily—no more alternating. Follow up with ENT for your nose and get an echo in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll schedule that. Should I stop the Miralax?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your nurse will review that. Avoid anything that causes loose stools. Stay hydrated and rise slowly from sitting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you feel dizzy, short of breath, or have chest pain. Otherwise, we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in today because of weakness and tingling in your arms and legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It’s been getting worse over the past few weeks. Today at my psychiatrist’s office, I could barely walk. They told me to go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. In the ER, they found your potassium was very high—8.3, which can definitely cause those symptoms. You were given treatment to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that high? I didn’t know potassium could do that. Is that why I felt so weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. High potassium affects your nerves and muscles. That’s why you had tingling and trouble walking. We’ve given you calcium, insulin, dextrose, albuterol, and a medication called Kayexalate to lower it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the IV insulin—I had a brief chest pressure then, in the back. It only lasted a few minutes and went away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. It wasn’t associated with shortness of breath or sweating, and your repeat heart tests were stable. It’s likely not heart-related, especially since you’ve never had chest pain before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why did my potassium go up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of end-stage renal disease and peritoneal dialysis, it’s likely your dialysis hasn’t been removing enough potassium. This can happen if the dialysis isn’t working as well as it should or if your body’s needs have changed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing my dialysis at home. Could something be wrong with the equipment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but we don’t have signs of infection in your peritoneal fluid, which is good. We’ll monitor your levels closely and make sure your dialysis is optimized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been feeling thirsty since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common after the insulin and dextrose treatment. Your body is adjusting. We’ll keep an eye on your fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach’s been cramping since I took that Kayexalate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a known side effect. It can cause constipation or cramping. Since you already have chronic constipation, we’ll make sure you’re still taking your lactulose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an abdominal X-ray this morning to check your dialysis catheter. It’s in the right place, and there’s no sign of a serious issue like a pneumoperitoneum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that when air gets into the belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It can happen with peritoneal dialysis, but your X-ray doesn’t show a large amount. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re not showing signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How’s my potassium now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much better. It came down to 4.8, which is in the normal range. Your EKG changes have also improved. The weakness and tingling should be gone now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel stronger. I walked to the bathroom earlier without help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ll keep you on close watch, but you’re definitely improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your labs and dialysis. Everything points to your high potassium being due to inadequate dialysis over the past few weeks, not an infection or other issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my dialysis at home wasn’t doing enough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It seems so. We don’t think the equipment is broken, but your body’s needs may have changed. Your nephrologist will help adjust your regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my other medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your lisinopril because it can raise potassium. Your blood pressure has been stable—around 110 systolic—so we didn’t restart it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I take it when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your outpatient provider should check your blood pressure first. If it’s still low, you may not need it right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re increasing your calcitriol to two tablets daily and your sevelamer to three tablets with each meal to better control your phosphate levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—those are for my bone and mineral balance, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. With ESRD, it’s important to keep those in check. Your other medications, like warfarin, fluoxetine, and mirtazapine, will stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your potassium is stable, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your nephrologist tomorrow to review your dialysis and labs. Make sure to have your blood pressure checked to see if you should restart lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new doses for calcitriol and sevelamer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start those as prescribed. Take sevelamer with meals to bind phosphate from food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if you feel weak, have tingling, or any new symptoms. Otherwise, keep up with your dialysis and follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. You’re cleared to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the neurology doctors. You were brought in after having a seizure. Can you tell me what happened before that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was lying in bed last night when I got this sudden headache—throbbing, across my forehead and top of my head. My blood pressure was 170 over 123, which is higher than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Did you notice anything else with the headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I started seeing flashing lights—colors, like rainbows—no matter where I looked. They lasted a couple minutes and kept coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Did you feel weak or numb anywhere?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My feet felt heavy, like I couldn’t lift them well. I didn’t think much of it at the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And then you called your nephrologist, took hydralazine, but symptoms didn’t go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I stayed in bed, but the pain kept waking me. This morning it was still there, so I called EMS.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When you arrived, you had another brief seizure and were given Ativan. You don’t remember that or the ambulance ride?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I don’t. I just remember waking up here, a bit confused at first, but I feel much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We did a CT scan of your head right away to rule out bleeding, and it was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But what caused the seizure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s related to very high blood pressure affecting your brain. We’re calling it hypertensive encephalopathy, or PRES for short.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: PRES? I’ve had that before—twice, actually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows that. That makes you more vulnerable. We’re doing an MRI to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI is back. It shows changes in the back parts of your brain—parietal and occipital lobes—consistent with PRES.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stroke or tumor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not a stroke or tumor. PRES is reversible with proper treatment. The main issue is your blood pressure and fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on peritoneal dialysis. Could that be part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your nephrologist thinks you’ve been retaining fluid, which raises your blood pressure. We’ll do a dialysis session tomorrow to remove extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure last night was still high—176 over 105. We’ve added verapamil to help protect your brain from spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on amlodipine at home. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started it yesterday, but your nephrologist prefers to stop it since your high BP is from fluid, not just vessel tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about metoprolol? I wasn’t taking it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you 50 mg yesterday, and your BP improved. We’ll send you home on 25 mg twice a day—lower dose, but consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for peritoneal dialysis at noon. It should help lower your blood pressure by removing excess fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How much fluid do you think I’m holding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hard to say exactly, but we expect several pounds. That should make a big difference in your BP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your blood pressure is much better today. It’s been running 130s over 80s since dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better too. No headache, no flashing lights.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neurologic exam is back to normal. That’s a good sign PRES is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the seizure? I’ve never had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was likely triggered by the brain swelling from high BP. But we also looked at your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take bupropion for depression. Could that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Bupropion can lower the seizure threshold, especially in someone with PRES. We’re cutting your dose in half for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop it completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless your psychiatrist says so. But please talk to them about whether a different antidepressant might be safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue most of your usual meds. Add verapamil three times a day, and take metoprolol 25 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bupropion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Half your usual dose—37.5 mg daily—for now. Also, your INR was a bit low, so tonight take 5 mg of warfarin, then go back to 4 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What if my blood pressure goes up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it’s over 160/100, go straight to the ER. Also call your nephrologist. This episode shows you’re at risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been nauseous a couple times today. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked. There’s mild tenderness near your dialysis catheter, but no signs of infection. It could be mild irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stay longer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome to stay a few more hours to monitor, but since you’re feeling better and vitals are stable, it’s okay to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to go home, but I’ll watch for worsening symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. If nausea returns, or you have fever, pain, or cloudy dialysis fluid, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care, and follow up with your doctors soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been feeling nauseous and have some abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. It started this morning—just after they said I could go home from the last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And where exactly is the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Around my belly button and near the dialysis catheter. It’s not sharp, just tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re concerned this could be related to your peritoneal dialysis. We’ll run some tests to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be an infection around the catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s one possibility. We call it peritonitis when the fluid in the abdomen gets infected. We’ll check your dialysis fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s serious, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re catching it early. We’ll start antibiotics just in case, even before we get all the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some mild atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—probably from shallow breathing. Nothing to worry about now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the nausea? I haven’t been taking deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll encourage you to use the incentive spirometer to help expand your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the repeat abdominal X-ray shows no free air. That rules out a bowel perforation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my bowels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The pain near your catheter and nausea point more toward a dialysis-related issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing IV antibiotics for possible peritonitis. How’s the nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not as bad. The pain is a little better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’ll keep monitoring your labs and dialysis fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis fluid came back with no white blood cells and no bacteria. That’s a good sign—no active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I still nauseous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not ruling out inflammation around the catheter. Even without infection, the area can get irritated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I still need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll finish the course since we started. But we’re also looking at other causes—like your recent PRES episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a drop in blood pressure and passed out earlier. We’re worried about access for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt dizzy and then everything went dark.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your INR was high, so we couldn’t place a line in your neck safely at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Coumadin for my lupus. Does that make bleeding more likely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. But the radiology team was able to place a dialysis line through a collateral vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can still get dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and that should help with fluid balance and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The blood cultures we drew came back negative. No sign of bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. It supports that this isn’t a widespread infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan showed no abscess or bowel issue. The fluid around your pancreas is likely from dialysis, though it’s in an unusual spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be causing the nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We checked your lipase and amylase—pancreas enzymes—and they’re normal, so no pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve repeated the blood cultures again—still no growth. You’re not running a fever, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re focusing on managing inflammation from the catheter and ensuring your dialysis is effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, and parasites. So it’s not a GI infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated too. Could that be part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Constipation can definitely contribute to nausea and discomfort. We’ll keep working on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRI brain results are back. The changes from PRES have completely resolved. No new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my brain is okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the swelling is gone. That’s great progress from your last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still feel nauseous when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Positional nausea can happen with inner ear issues or even residual effects from PRES. But we’re not seeing anything dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been stable. We’re continuing your current antihypertensives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lupus and kidney transplant history—are they playing a role?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lupus and failed transplant increase your risk for complications, but right now, the catheter site inflammation is the main focus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking better. The nausea is improving, and your labs are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We want to make sure your dialysis access is secure and symptoms don’t return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray confirms your peritoneal catheter is still in good position. No kinks or movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it might be causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause irritation, but it’s not displaced. We’ll keep managing the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gone two days without nausea. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any return of nausea, fever, or increased tenderness around the catheter. If so, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Coumadin and other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all as prescribed. Follow up with your nephrologist and hematologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your labs are stable, no infection signs, and you’re tolerating oral intake well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you tomorrow morning. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in after having chest pain during dialysis. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, during dialysis my blood pressure dropped—nurse said it was 103 in my ankle. I felt awful, like I was going to pass out or die. Then right after they gave me saline, I got this heavy, sharp pain in the center of my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And it was accompanied by shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it radiated a bit to my jaw. I always get left jaw pain during dialysis, but never chest pain like this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The EMTs gave you aspirin and nitroglycerin—did those help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. But the pain did go away mostly by the time I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked your cardiac enzymes twice already, and they’re normal. Your EKG also hasn’t changed from your prior ones. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely to be a heart attack, but we’re still being cautious. We did a CT scan to rule out a pulmonary embolism, which also came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. But the CT did show something else—we saw signs that might suggest a clot in your left subclavian vein. We’ll need an ultrasound to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A clot? But I’m on dialysis and have lupus and APS—I’ve had clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your antiphospholipid syndrome puts you at higher risk for clots, but you also have a bleeding tendency due to your platelet issue. So we have to be very careful with treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. It’s always a balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted hematology and your transplant team. We’ll monitor you closely and likely start anticoagulation carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound confirmed clots in your left internal jugular, axillary, and one of the brachial veins. They’re non-occlusive, which means blood is still flowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s serious, but not blocking everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. But we still need to treat it to prevent it from growing or breaking off. We’re starting you on a heparin drip, and we’ll transition you to warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Coumadin before. But won’t that increase my bleeding risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, which is why we’re monitoring your Factor Xa levels instead of PTT, and adjusting the heparin every six hours. Once your INR is stable on warfarin, we’ll stop the IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your dialysis session. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but okay. No chest pain this time. My arm feels a bit heavy though—left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be related to the clot. We’ll keep monitoring. We also gave you non-invasive ventilation earlier to support your breathing—did you notice that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the mask. It helped. I felt a bit short of breath when I first came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your creatinine dropped from 5.6 to 4.1 after dialysis—that’s great. Your hemoglobin is stable, though still on the lower side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of my anemia from kidney disease?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s part of it. We’re continuing your usual meds, including calcitriol and phosphate binders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my migraine yesterday—was that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We gave you Fioricet, and it resolved. Your neurologist thinks your diplopia and migraines may be related to lamotrigine, but we’re keeping it for seizure prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have an update. Your IV in the left hand infiltrated, so we lost access. We’ve had a team discussion—given your bleeding risk, we’re switching to subcutaneous heparin injections three times a day while we bridge to warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Injections? I can do that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. A nurse will teach you. Once your INR is therapeutic on warfarin, we’ll stop the injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And how long until that happens?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a few days. We’ll check your INR daily, then more often once you’re on warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.1—almost therapeutic. We’ve reduced the subcutaneous heparin and will keep adjusting your warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Getting closer. We want your INR stable for at least a day or two. And we need to make sure your chest pain doesn’t return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any since that first episode. But should I get another stress test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your last one was negative less than a year ago, and your enzymes were normal. It’s likely not cardiac. But we recommend you follow up with your PCP or cardiologist about a nuclear stress test, especially since you have leg pain with walking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.8—solidly in range. We’ve stopped the subcutaneous heparin. You’re now fully on warfarin 3 mg nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So when do I get discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll do one more dialysis session, and if all goes well, you can go home the day after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You completed dialysis without issues. Your physical exam is stable—lungs clear, heart regular, no swelling in your arms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my malar rash—is that from lupus flaring?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. But it’s mild, and you’re not having other signs of flare—no joint pain or fever. We’ll continue your usual lupus management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my stomach is a bit tender—epigastric and right upper side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. It could be from gastritis or your GERD. We’re keeping you on omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your INR held at 2.6, and you’ve had no complications. We’re planning discharge tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications, especially warfarin at 3 mg nightly. Have your INR checked at every dialysis session—three times a week—and the results will be sent to your nephrologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my INR is too high or low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The dialysis team will alert your doctor. Don’t adjust the dose yourself. Also, watch for signs of bleeding—unusual bruising, blood in urine or stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my chest pain—should I go to the ER if it comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially if it’s severe or with shortness of breath. But given your normal tests, it’s likely not cardiac. Still, better safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your PCP soon. They’ll decide if you need a stress test. Also keep your nephrology and lupus appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is confirmed for this afternoon. We’ve updated your medication list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—warfarin is new. And your sodium polystyrene dose has increased to 15 grams twice a week. Everything else remains the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure my pharmacy has that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—should I avoid certain foods with warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, try to keep your vitamin K intake consistent—so no sudden increases in leafy greens. But you don’t need to avoid them completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up, and remember—call if you have chest pain, bleeding, or your weight increases by more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. Your condition is stable, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe, and we’ll coordinate your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you leave. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling the same—tired but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember to use your CPAP at night and keep taking your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge summary mentions chest pain of uncertain origin and the upper extremity DVTs. But you’re in good shape to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll follow up like we discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and we’ll see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is ready. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your records are sent to your nephrologist and PCP. INR monitoring is set up at dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I feel prepared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll be in touch if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’ve received all your discharge instructions and medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s here. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll be in touch if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really weak, especially in my legs. I also felt unbalanced, like I might fall. My PCP thought my potassium might be high again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium came back at 6.0, which is high. That can definitely cause weakness and fatigue. We’ve started treating it with calcium, insulin, and glucose through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. I’ve had this before. But I also had a fever a few days ago and still have a dry cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned chills and a low-grade fever since your last discharge. We’ll keep an eye on that. Your chest X-ray shows some mild fluid buildup in the lungs, which could be from heart strain or fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be pneumonia? I’ve had infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t look like pneumonia. The changes are more consistent with mild pulmonary edema, likely from fluid retention. We’ll manage that with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m due for dialysis today, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be going for hemodialysis this evening. That will help bring your potassium down and remove excess fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel a little better already, but my legs are still weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your muscle enzymes because your nephrologist is concerned about possible muscle injury from electrolyte shifts. Your aldolase was elevated, and LDH was high, but CK was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean? Is something wrong with my muscles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not clear yet. The pattern could be related to your lupus or fluid shifts. We’ll follow up with your rheumatologist to see if further evaluation is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
