conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I’ve also noticed my left hand is more swollen and painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed that. Your left hand is cyanotic and swollen up to the elbow. This could be related to your dialysis fistula or possibly your previous DVT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that clot in my arm last time. Is it getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was therapeutic when you came in, so your warfarin is working. We’ll keep monitoring the swelling. It may be due to poor flow through the fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about losing the fistula?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it closely. If there’s concern about clotting, your nephrology team may consider imaging. For now, we’ll keep your anticoagulation going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And I should keep taking the warfarin every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. You’ll need to have your INR checked three times a week during dialysis. Your nephrologist will monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your potassium is now 3.1 after dialysis, which is much better. Your creatinine also dropped from 9.3 to 3.6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel stronger already, though my legs are still a bit shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your labs show improvement, and there’s no sign of new neurological issues. We still think this is related to the high potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my cough and fever? I still feel a little warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your temperature has been normal since admission, and your white count is stable. The cough and lung changes are likely from fluid, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s not an infection. I’ve been through that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we reviewed your history. You’ve got a lot going on—lupus, ESRD, clotting issues—but we’re managing everything step by step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my double vision? I haven’t mentioned it, but it’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s been noted and is thought to be related to your lamotrigine. Neurology is aware, and you’re still on the same dose, which is important for seizure control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I just wanted to make sure it wasn’t something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to bring up. Always let us know if symptoms change. Now, your plan today is to continue monitoring and prepare for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Discharge? So soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because your potassium is stable, you’re feeling better, and your main issues are managed. You’ll go home and continue your regular dialysis schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your labs are stable, and you’re no longer weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your medications, especially warfarin. Have your INR checked at every dialysis session and call if your weight increases by more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about the muscle test results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are still pending. Your rheumatologist will follow up with you. If there’s any concern, they’ll let you know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You’ve been admitted because of worsening hand ischemia from your right arm dialysis fistula. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes, my hand’s been cold and numb, especially when I use it. It’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called steal syndrome. The fistula is pulling too much blood away from your hand. We’re planning a procedure called fistula banding to reduce the flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my dialysis? I need that fistula to work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’ll narrow the fistula just enough to restore blood to your hand while keeping it usable for dialysis. There’s a small risk it could clot, but saving your hand comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. When will this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today. First, we’ll get you prepped and review the consent. You’ll have hemodialysis first, as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had dialysis this morning already. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was outpatient. Today’s session will be after your procedure, to keep your fluids and electrolytes balanced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my warfarin? I’m on blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held your warfarin temporarily to reduce bleeding risk during surgery. We’ll restart it soon after, once we’re sure there’s no bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I was worried about clots with my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re being careful. You’ll get heparin shots while off warfarin to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from the procedure. The banding was successful. We narrowed the fistula, and your radial pulse is now strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How does my hand feel? It still feels cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a good sign it’s still cold right now—means we reduced the flow enough. It should warm up over the next few hours as circulation adjusts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It aches a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you Vicodin for pain. Keep your arm elevated on pillows to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, since I took the medicine. My hand feels a little warmer too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. You’ll have dialysis in a few hours. We’ll monitor your potassium and fluids closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You finished dialysis well. Your vitals are stable, and labs look good. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Should I still take my other meds like mirtazapine and quetiapine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued all your regular medications except warfarin, which we’ll restart tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your hand is warmer, and the pulse is strong. We’re going to restart warfarin at a lower dose today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the fistula still working? I feel a buzz, but is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the buzzing is a good sign—means blood is flowing. We checked with ultrasound; the fistula is open and functioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my other arm? I have a fistula there too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both fistulas are intact. For dialysis, they’ll use the right one to pull blood and the left to return it—‘1 and 1’ setup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is starting to rise, which means the warfarin is working. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lupus and kidney issues? Are they stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lupus is quiet, and your dialysis is managing your kidney failure well. The main issue was the hand ischemia, which we’ve addressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if everything stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on your hand. If it turns cold, blue, or you can’t move it, call us. Also watch for fever, pus, or heavy bleeding from the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it dry for two days. After that, you can remove it and shower. Steri-strips will fall off on their own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain medicine? I still have some ache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with hydrocodone for a few days. Don’t take it longer than three days unless we say so. It can cause constipation—so we’re adding docusate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and when do I see the surgeon again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about two weeks. Call the office to schedule. Also, weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re alert, pain is controlled, and your hand is warm with good pulses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: no lifting over 10 pounds for three days, no heavy exercise for two weeks, and start fistula exercises in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no blood pressure checks or IVs in the access arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve got it. Call us with any concerns. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your prescriptions and discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve got my pills and the instructions. I’ll follow up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping care for you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was fine until this morning. I bent over to pick something up and suddenly felt dizzy—like lightheaded and off-balance. I couldn’t walk without help, so I had to use a wheelchair at my pulmonologist’s office.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you lose consciousness or feel any numbness, weakness, or trouble speaking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I stayed awake, but I felt confused—like my judgment wasn’t right. I’ve also been more tired than usual and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We ran a CT scan of your head to rule out a stroke. It didn’t show any bleeding or stroke, but there is some inflammation in your sinuses. That might be contributing, but it’s not the main issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stroke? But why did I feel so off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neurology saw you and agreed it’s not an acute stroke. Your NIH stroke score was zero. But we noticed you missed your dialysis session today. Your labs show your creatinine is high—6.6—which means your body is holding onto waste products.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that makes sense. I’ve had confusion like this before when I miss dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We think this is a toxic metabolic encephalopathy—basically, the buildup of toxins affecting your brain. It’s common in ESRD when dialysis is delayed. We’ll get you dialyzed as soon as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But I’ve also had a headache and my right eye has been bothering me—pain and blurry vision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ll get ophthalmology to see you for that. It could be keratitis—an inflammation or infection of the cornea. We’ll treat it with antibiotic drops if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The eye doctor saw you. They diagnosed keratitis and prescribed moxifloxacin eye drops four times a day for seven days, plus erythromycin ointment at night for irritation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that clear up my vision?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, most likely. You’ll need to follow up in their clinic to see if steroid drops are needed later. Avoid rubbing your eye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had dialysis last night. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The dizziness is gone, and I’m thinking more clearly. But I still feel a bit unsteady on my feet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. Neurology thinks your imbalance is chronic and multifactorial. It could be due to fluid shifts during dialysis affecting your inner ear, or mild spinal arthritis in your neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything I can do about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Try wearing a soft cervical collar during dialysis and keep your head neutral. Also, compression stockings may help prevent blood pressure drops that worsen dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can try that. What about the crackles in my lungs? I heard the nurse mention that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray showed mild pulmonary edema and a small pleural effusion. That’s likely from fluid buildup due to kidney failure. Dialysis should help clear that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No infection then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. Your white count is normal, and you don’t have fever or cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your INR this morning. It was low at 1.8, below your goal of 2.5. Since you’re on warfarin for a past DVT, we’ve increased your dose from 3 mg to 4 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m worried about bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re staying within the safe range. Your goal is 1.5 to 2.5. At 4 mg, we expect it to come up just right. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs show your creatinine dropped to 4.9 and urea to 28—much better after dialysis. Your hemoglobin also improved slightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Physical therapy saw you and says you can walk with a walker. You’ll have home physical therapy set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve been feeling like I’m not getting good care here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you, and I’m sorry you’ve felt that way. Our goal is to stabilize you and get you back to your routine safely. We’re on track for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had your second dialysis session last night. Your symptoms continue to improve. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular medications. Use the eye drops as prescribed. Wear compression stockings during dialysis and consider the neck collar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my weight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Weigh yourself every morning. Call your doctor if you gain more than three pounds in a day—that could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are stable. You’re cleared for discharge. Your sister will help you at home, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’s on her way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume your MWF dialysis schedule. Follow up with your nephrologist, eye doctor, and get home physical therapy. Keep taking the warfarin at 4 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to get out of here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain started during my dialysis session. It’s diffuse, and it hurts more when I eat or move. Even lying on the bed felt painful last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned rebound tenderness—when you press and let go, it hurts more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s what worried me. The car ride here was awful—every bump made it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your CT scan. Good news—it’s not appendicitis or anything surgical. You have a condition called epiploic appendagitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Epiploic what? I’ve never heard of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s inflammation of a small fat tag on the colon. It can cause sharp pain, especially in the lower abdomen. It’s not dangerous and usually resolves on its own in about a week or ten days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So it’s not my lupus or kidneys acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is separate. Your labs and dialysis status are stable. Your creatinine is a bit high, but not concerning since you’re due for dialysis soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also started having joint pain—shoulders and thumbs. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely to be from the abdominal issue. You mentioned it doesn’t feel like your usual lupus flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s different. But the pain in my right hand feels a bit like my old gout attacks, just milder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. We didn’t see signs of acute gout, but it could be an early flare. I’d recommend following up with your PCP about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. So no surgery or special treatment needed for the belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. It gets better on its own. We’ll send you home with a short supply of oxycodone to use if the pain flares up, but many people don’t even need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your regular medications, including warfarin, blood pressure pills, and omeprazole. We’ve listed them in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. And when can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once we confirm your pain is stable and you’re comfortable. We expect to discharge you later this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look stable, and you’re feeling better. We’re clearing you to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Just to confirm—rest, watch the pain, and follow up with my doctor about the joint issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if the pain worsens or you develop fever, vomiting, or new symptoms. Otherwise, it should resolve on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll keep an eye on it and see my PCP next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and stay hydrated. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all your help, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel better than yesterday. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take it easy and rest up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started in my back while I was paying bills. I wasn’t sure if it was just muscle pain, but then it moved to my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you have any shortness of breath or neck pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a little shortness of breath and some neck discomfort. I took my nitroglycerin, but it didn’t help much—and I felt dizzy afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Because of your history of esophageal spasms, we think this might be related to that, not your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it felt different this time. Shouldn’t we check the heart just in case?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did. Your EKG was normal, and your troponin levels were slightly elevated, but that’s typical for you because of your kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. What about the CT scan I had?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed no blood clot in your lungs. There’s mild fluid in the lungs, but it’s unchanged from before. No sign of infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s probably my esophagus again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, most likely. The pain pattern and your history point to esophageal spasm. We’ll keep monitoring you tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No chest pain at all. I’ve been walking around and feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We reviewed with the kidney team. You don’t need dialysis tonight just for the contrast—you can go to your regular session tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about that. What about my warfarin? I take it for my blood clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was a bit low, but since you’re stopping warfarin soon for surgery anyway, we’re not changing the dose or adding a bridge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Should I still use the nitroglycerin if the chest pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but call your GI doctor to discuss better control of your esophageal spasms. If the pain is severe or different, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Should I keep taking them all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your home medications as usual. We’ve sent the list to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My right hand is really tender today—more than usual. Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Given your history of gout and steroid use, it could be a flare. Keep an eye on it and mention it to your rheumatologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send you with instructions and your updated med list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. You’re here today for a planned procedure on your right arm fistula because of steal syndrome, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My hand’s been cold and painful for weeks. It gets worse after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Steal syndrome means too much blood is going into the fistula and not enough to your hand. We’re going to do a banding procedure to reduce the flow and help your hand get more blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this done before. It helped for a while. Is this the same thing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the same procedure—banding the fistula. It’s less invasive than removing it completely. We hope it will relieve your symptoms again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can still use the fistula for dialysis after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the goal—to keep it working for dialysis while fixing the hand pain. We’ll check it after the procedure and again tomorrow during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’m a little nervous, but I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take good care of you. You’ll go to the operating room around noon. After that, you’ll wake up in the recovery area, then come back here to your room.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. How are you feeling after the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit groggy, but okay. My arm feels tight, but not painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ve banded the fistula, and the dressing is snug. You’ll get pain medicine if you need it. We’ll also check your hand’s color and warmth often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat? I’m kind of hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can have a regular diet. We’ll start you on your home medications too, including your blood thinner, warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I take a lot of meds, but I brought my list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed it. Everything’s been restarted except your dialysis schedule, which will be tomorrow as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s your hand feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s warmer than it’s been in weeks! The pain is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. It means the banding is working. We’ll keep monitoring it. Any chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not today. I had some last week, but it went away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray just to be safe. It showed clear lungs and no issues. Your heart size is normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried it might be my heart again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, we always check. But this time, it’s not cardiac. Your labs also look stable—your kidney function is as expected for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, can I take my pain meds? My arm is starting to ache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can take the Dilaudid as needed. Two milligrams every four hours. Let us know if it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also take tramadol sometimes. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stick with Dilaudid for now since it’s stronger and works faster. We can switch back to tramadol when you’re home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You slept well? We’re going to do some blood work before dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I did. Is the dialysis still scheduled for today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, at noon. We want to make sure the fistula works well after the banding. So far, the thrill is strong and your hand is warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it might not work after the surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We monitored it closely. The banding reduced flow just enough to help your hand without killing the fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great during dialysis. The team said the fistula functioned well, and your blood pressure stayed stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel dizzy or weak like I sometimes do. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And your hand is still warm and pink. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the access clinic if your hand becomes cold, blue, or painful, or if you can’t feel the thrill. Also for fever, swelling, or if the dressing gets wet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? Should I change anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, go back to all your usual medications. We adjusted your warfarin dose slightly—now 3 mg daily. Your outpatient team will check your INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No heavy lifting, no blood pressure checks on my arms, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Protect both arms. Wear loose sleeves and no tight jewelry. Follow up with your surgeon in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad the procedure helped. You’ll be discharged in a few hours once the paperwork is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only mild discomfort. I took acetaminophen earlier and it helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep using acetaminophen for mild pain. Save the Dilaudid for if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep doing dialysis as usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly on schedule. The fistula is working well, so no changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad this is behind me. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping care for you during your stay. You were admitted because of high potassium, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s what they told me. I’ve had this before—felt weak in my legs, shaky. It’s scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your potassium was very high—7.6—so we gave you some treatment in the ER to protect your heart and then started dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember getting insulin and sugar. I felt worse for a bit—my blood sugar dropped, didn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your sugar went low after the insulin, down to the 20s. We gave you dextrose and juice, and it came back up. You’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been doing all my dialysis, taking my kayexalate. I don’t know why this happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re trying to figure out. You’ve had normal diets and no missed treatments. One clue is your INR was low—1.4—when it should be between 1.5 and 2.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on warfarin for my antiphospholipid syndrome. My dose is a bit confusing—3 and 4 mg on different days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your nephrologist thinks the low INR might be linked to the high potassium. We’ll adjust your warfarin to 5 mg daily to keep it in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. But I also had belly pain earlier. Is that gone for good?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your abdominal pain has resolved. We did a CT scan to check for serious causes like bowel ischemia, but everything looked okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the little blood on the toilet paper? Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very minimal, and no other signs of bleeding. With your history of hysterectomy, it’s likely from the rectal area. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve also been on levofloxacin for sinusitis. They stopped it in the ER, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Potassium is down to 5.2 after dialysis, which is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT results back. No bleeding or bowel issues. Also saw some small cysts in your pancreas, but they’re likely harmless.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with transplant surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists taking care of you tonight. You're here because of worsening shortness of breath and fatigue. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.text: What’s the plan then?

conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ACE wrap?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for anything at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.text: No signs of new clots. Your history of DVT is well-managed with warfarin. We’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It’s usually high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable—around 110/50. We’ll keep you on amlodipine and labetolol, but skip the morning dose on dialysis days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that. What about my other meds? Can I take them as usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your medications are continued. We’ve kept your list the same, including kayexalate three times a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been using the eye drops and creams regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The dizziness is almost gone, and I walked to the bathroom without trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your neurologic exam is normal. We think this was an acute flare of your chronic dizziness, possibly migraine-related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more tests? I’m safe to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you tomorrow. You’ll follow up with your PCP and have dialysis as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your symptoms have resolved, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Any final instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all medications, especially warfarin and kayexalate. Get the MRCP done as planned. And consider cognitive testing if you’re concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if dizziness returns or if you feel unwell. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's been sharp and in the upper middle area. It started after that ERCP procedure earlier today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The ERCP was done because of a bile duct stone, but they couldn’t remove it due to a tight opening. We’re concerned you may have developed pancreatitis as a result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pancreatitis? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. Your lipase level is very high—over 20,000—so we’ll keep you NPO, meaning no food or drink by mouth, to let your pancreas rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. But I’m on dialysis—will that still happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll still get dialysis tomorrow as scheduled. We’ll manage your fluids carefully. We also stopped your warfarin before the ERCP, but we’ll restart it soon since you’re not having bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m worried about clots. I’ve had DVTs before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly why we need to restart it. For now, we’re watching closely. We’ll do a CT scan tonight to confirm the pancreatitis and check for complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT confirmed acute pancreatitis. There’s inflammation around the pancreas, and your liver enzymes are elevated. But no necrosis or abscess—good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO for a few more days. You’ll get IV fluids and pain meds. Once your pain and labs improve, we’ll start you on clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m already feeling bloated. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw some ileus on the X-ray—slowed bowel movement. It’s common with pancreatitis. We’ll monitor it and help with stool softeners later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but the pain is a bit better. I had a fever last night though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. Your white count didn’t go up, and blood cultures are negative. Likely from inflammation, not infection. We started antibiotics briefly but will stop them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hand is swollen. We did an ultrasound—no clot, but your dialysis graft flow is very slow. It’s likely failing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Does that mean I need a new access?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll discuss with your nephrologist. For now, we’re using your tunneled catheter for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lipase is coming down, and you’re less tender. We’re going to try a clear liquid diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally! Can I have broth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, small sips at first. We’ll watch for any increase in pain or nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows your bowels are moving better. Ileus is improving. You’ve been passing gas—that’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel constipated. The pain meds are making it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding docusate and senna to help. We’ll also reduce narcotics if possible. We don’t want to over-sedate you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a strange episode last night—talking about shadows and people in the room. The nurse said you were alert but paranoid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I saw them! I know it sounds crazy, but I was scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon with severe illness, pain, and narcotics. Psychiatry thinks it’s delirium. They recommend continuing trazodone for sleep but avoiding stronger sedatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel normal again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re getting there. Your labs are improving. Creatinine is down to 3.9, and liver enzymes are trending better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your diet is advancing to soft solids. And your INR is stable, so we’re restarting warfarin at 2 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a low dose, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll titrate up. You’ll need daily INR checks at dialysis until it’s in the 1.5–2.5 range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re moving your bowels now—great. We can stop the senna if you’re having more than three stools a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still having back pain. Is that from the pancreas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. But your chronic back pain and anxiety might be making it feel worse. We’re adding lidocaine patches for relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anxiety for years. It flares when I’m sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry agrees. They suggested quetiapine, but you declined due to tardive dyskinesia concerns. That’s understandable. Keep following up with your therapist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lipase is now 40—completely normal. And your abdomen is soft with no tenderness. We’re almost ready to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s wonderful!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll schedule your ERCP as an outpatient. No urgent need—the stone isn’t blocking anything now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis access needs evaluation. The vascular team will see you soon to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about another surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take it step by step. For now, your catheter is working fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds, plus warfarin 2 mg daily, lidocaine patches for back pain, and docusate and senna for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain med?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hydromorphone, but now every 4 hours as needed, not every 6. Use it sparingly to avoid constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last check—your INR is 2.1. Perfect. We’ll switch to weekly checks after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eyes and skin—should I keep using those creams?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual skin and eye treatments. And don’t forget your dialysis and follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. A nurse will go over your meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Remember: follow up with your PCP, nephrologist, and mental health provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave, any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—should I worry about the pancreatitis coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The main risk was the stone, which we’ll address later. For now, stay hydrated, avoid heavy meals, and take your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if you have fever, severe pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. You’re discharged with home services for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister will help at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Keep up the progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be your doctor during this stay. You were admitted because of weight loss and poor appetite. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve lost a lot of weight—down to 40 kilograms from 50 just a month ago. I feel full quickly, my mouth tastes strange, and I’ve been nauseous. I can’t keep food or even pills down sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you were taking pancreatic enzymes at home to help with eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but they made me more nauseous. I stopped them yesterday because I couldn’t keep them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. We’ll hold off on those for now. We’ll check your labs and get Nutrition involved to help figure out what you can tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m just so weak. I don’t know if it’s from not eating or something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s very likely from the weight loss and poor intake. We’ll make sure you’re getting enough calories and monitor your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your kidney function is expected for someone on dialysis. Your hemoglobin is a bit low, but stable. We’re watching your electrolytes closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my INR okay? I’m on warfarin for blood clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low—only 1.1. That means your blood isn’t thin enough, which increases clot risk. We’re starting a heparin drip to bridge you until the warfarin kicks in better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize. Could that be why I’ve been feeling off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might contribute, but your symptoms are more likely from poor nutrition. We’ll keep the heparin going until your INR is above 1.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nutrition team met with you. They said you’re doing better with clear Nepro and small, frequent meals. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the clear version doesn’t make me nauseous. But I worry—getting groceries is hard for me at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging for elder services to help with grocery assistance after discharge. That should make it easier to keep eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be a big help. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 1.4. Still a bit low, but improving. We’ll keep the heparin going a bit longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? Being on both heparin and warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s standard. Heparin works fast, warfarin takes days. We overlap them to prevent clots during the transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain has improved, and you’re tolerating a regular diet. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel like I can eat again. But I’m still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body’s recovering. We’ll keep monitoring your labs and strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had dialysis yesterday as scheduled. Your potassium was high before—5.4—but came down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always worry about that. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: High potassium can affect your heart, but dialysis helps remove it. We monitor closely, so you’re safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 1.6—within the target range. We’ll stop the heparin drip today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great! So I’m protected from clots now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood is thin enough. We’ll keep your warfarin adjusted to stay in that range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight is stable at 42 kg. That’s a good sign your intake is sufficient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was scared I’d keep losing weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. The combination of nutrition support and home assistance should help you maintain it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your bloodwork. Your liver enzymes are normal, which is good—no sign of active pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the abdominal pain isn’t from that anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it seems resolved. The pain you had was likely from the recent pancreatitis, but it’s healing now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low when you stood up yesterday—orthostatic. We held your labetalol temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get dizzy when I stand. Should I stop that medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll restart it at a lower dose—100 mg twice daily. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on lamotrigine for seizures and omeprazole for reflux. Both are important to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t had any double vision lately. I think the dose is okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Neurology has you on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your warfarin as adjusted—3 mg five times a week, 4 mg twice a week. Get your INR checked at dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the clear Nepro and small meals. Elder services will contact you about grocery help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to weigh myself daily, like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day—could be fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your physical exam today shows you’re strong, alert, and your abdomen is soft and not tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. We’ll finalize discharge papers today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge summary is ready. You’re going home with a plan to maintain nutrition and anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health meds—trazodone—I’ll keep taking that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue as needed for anxiety. We didn’t change any of your psychiatric meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Any nausea or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m feeling steady. Eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll see you at discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your final INR is 1.6—perfect. All your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: INR check at dialysis, daily weights, and follow up with your providers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge orders are in. You’ll get a copy of your updated med list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll review it with my pharmacist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. And call us if anything changes—especially weight or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Time to go home. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. Call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve confirmed your ride is here. You’re officially discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: your weight stayed stable, you’re eating well, and your INR is therapeutic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep working on it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming everything is in order before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all set. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge complete. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re going home stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too. I’m looking forward to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve earned it. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with dizziness and weakness this morning. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, around 8 a.m. I was making breakfast and suddenly felt like I was losing balance in all directions. I didn’t fall, but I had to sit down. My right hand felt weak, and I couldn’t dial the phone correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Did you have any headache at that time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not then. But I got a headache later in the afternoon after arriving at the ER. I’ve also had nausea, but no vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And the dizziness—did it feel like spinning or more like unsteadiness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It wasn’t spinning. It was like I was moving and the room was moving with me, but not turning. It got worse when I moved my head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see you also mentioned double vision. Is that still happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better now. At first, it was in all directions, even looking straight. Now it only happens when I look to the left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Your potassium level came back high—7.1—which can cause weakness and confusion. You were given calcium, insulin, and glucose in the ER. Did you notice your symptoms improving after that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, actually. Most of it got better after I got those treatments and then after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also did a CT scan of your head to rule out stroke or bleeding. The results showed no acute issues—no stroke or hemorrhage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But what caused all this then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a combination of factors. Your BUN was over 100, which means you’re uremic—your body is holding onto waste products. That can cause confusion and weakness. The high potassium didn’t help. But given your history of migraines, neurology thinks this could be an atypical migraine episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do get migraines, but not usually like this. No severe headache at the start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Some migraines don’t start with pain—they can present with dizziness, confusion, or vision changes. This might have been a ‘migraine equivalent.’ Your symptoms improving after dialysis supports that it was also related to uremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My heart rate was really low in the ER—down to 35. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but in your case, it’s likely due to the high potassium affecting your heart’s rhythm. Your ECG showed peaked T-waves, which is a sign of that. After treatment and dialysis, your potassium dropped to 5.6 and your heart rate normalized.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on the monitor now. Will I need it all night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on telemetry overnight just to be safe. But since your heart rate has been stable, we may remove it tomorrow. I see you have a skin reaction to adhesives—any issues with the leads?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had rashes before. The nurse put some cream on, which helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had dialysis this morning. Your potassium is now 4.3, and creatinine improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I felt short of breath yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in today because of dizziness, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. I woke up with it this morning—worse when I move my head. And this morning around 10:30, I suddenly felt very dizzy and had trouble speaking for a minute or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds scary. But the good news is, we did a CT scan of your head and it showed no stroke or bleeding. Neurology also saw you in the ER and said your symptoms are consistent with a problem in your inner ear—what we call peripheral vestibulopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve had dizziness before, but this time I also felt unsteady in my arms. Is that part of it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned ataxia—clumsiness in your arms. But the neurology team didn’t find any signs of a stroke or cerebellar issue. Your exam showed a positive head thrust to the right, which supports the inner ear diagnosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a stroke? I was really worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’re confident it’s not a stroke. NIHSS score was zero, and imaging was completely normal. Your symptoms improved after dialysis, which also supports this being related to your usual vestibular issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a bit better after dialysis earlier today. But why am I being admitted if it’s just my usual dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. In the ER, your heart rate dropped to about 50 beats per minute, and you said you felt lightheaded. That’s called symptomatic bradycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I did feel my heart was slow. But it’s better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, during dialysis your heart rate came up to 70–80, and you said you felt closer to your baseline. The team thinks your blood pressure medication—amlodipine—may have contributed, especially with your electrolyte levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take amlodipine for high blood pressure. Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re keeping you on the same dose—5 mg daily—for now. But we’ll watch your heart rate closely. Since you’re on dialysis, potassium and other electrolytes can affect your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My potassium was high earlier, wasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 7.0 when you arrived, which is quite high. That can definitely affect heart function. But after dialysis, it dropped to 4.5 this morning—much safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I didn’t realize potassium could do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. High potassium makes the heart more irritable and can slow it down. Dialysis helped clear that, along with your creatinine, which dropped from 7.9 to 5.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So dialysis helped both my dizziness and my heart rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It corrected your electrolytes and likely reduced some fluid shifts that can worsen dizziness. You’re feeling more stable on your feet now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I walked to the bathroom earlier without any trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Your neuro exam today shows no focal deficits. You’re walking well, no instability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my warfarin? I take it for my blood clots history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on 3 mg daily, and your INR was 1.6—within your target range of 1.5 to 2.5. We continued it as usual. No bleeding concerns this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last time I was in, I had bleeding after an ERCP. I was worried it might happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I reviewed your last admission. That was a complication from the procedure, but you’ve had no GI symptoms this time—no melena or abdominal pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my seizure medicine—lamotrigine—is still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing lamotrigine. Neurology has followed your diplopia, and there’s no change. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Dizziness is mostly gone. I’m just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’ve had a long day with dialysis and all the evaluations. We’ll keep monitoring your vitals tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have your labs back. Your potassium is normal, kidney function improved, and your blood count is stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Do I need to change any of my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No major changes. We’re keeping your amlodipine, warfarin, and all other meds the same. One small change—your ranitidine dose is now 150 mg at night instead of 300.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Should I watch for anything after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If the dizziness returns severely, or if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or pass black stools, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dialysis schedule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue as usual. Your nephrologist will follow up on your anemia and pancytopenia as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with your doctors as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had this pain in my lower left belly for about a day. It started off and on but now it’s constant. I also had nausea and threw up once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but I did feel chills. And my right shoulder started hurting too, which worried me because I’ve been on antibiotics for a sinus infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And how’s your appetite been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not good. I haven’t been eating much because I feel nauseous. I passed a bowel movement this morning and I’m passing gas, but I haven’t urinated at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense given your kidney condition. We’ll check a CT scan to see what’s going on in your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also felt really weak this morning—like I couldn’t stand up when I was at my doctor’s office.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that could be from dehydration or electrolyte imbalances. We’ve already drawn some labs, and your potassium is high, which we expect with your dialysis schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I missed my last dialysis because I was in the ER. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with high potassium. But we’ll get you dialyzed soon. Your heart rhythm is stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. What about the shoulder pain? Could it be from the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray, and there’s no fracture. It looks like bursitis—likely inflammation. The levofloxacin can sometimes cause tendon issues, so we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop the antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You already stopped it three days ago, and since you don’t have sinus drainage, we’ll hold off. We’ll recommend saline spray instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. It shows a lot of stool in your colon and some distended bowel loops. We think you have an ileus—basically, your bowels are sluggish, likely from not eating and the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection or blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No blockage. The scan doesn’t show that. But the findings are consistent with mild gastroenteritis, which may have started this whole thing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sister had nausea and vomiting too—maybe it’s going around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. We’ll treat it as such. We’re starting you on a bowel regimen—laxatives like senna, Colace, and a few others to help get things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on some of those before. Will I be able to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’d like you to try a regular diet. We’ll give you Zofran for nausea if it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The belly pain is less, and I haven’t felt nauseous since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. You had dialysis yesterday, and your potassium came down from 6.8 to 4.6—much safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a bit dizzy during dialysis. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
